      "markdown": "# New ways to supervise, inspect, and constrain coding agents

As-of: 2026-10-14

**Presentation direction:** Planned for synthetic narration. Retain the spoken AI disclosure. Use simple diagrams and clearly labeled illustrative screens, not fabricated product demonstrations. Evidence annotations are not spoken.

**Visual direction:** Title card, date, and three columns: “Supervision,” “Secret checking,” and “Diagnosis.”

**Narration:**
This presentation uses AI-generated narration. As of October 14, 2026, some of the most concrete coding-assistant developments concern how you supervise an agent and inspect its work—not demonstrated improvements in coding quality. For someone building a small app or script, that distinction matters. Access lets you direct work. Checks flag possible problems. Diagnostic artifacts help you investigate. None of these, on its own, establishes that your project is finished or safe.

**Visual direction:** Diagram connecting a phone to an agent running on a computer. Keep the label “Computer must stay on and online” visible.

**Narration:**
First, supervision. Cursor announced that its iOS app can display local agents running on your computer and accept replies. The important qualification is where execution happens: the agent stays on your computer. Remote control does not move that work elsewhere, and your computer must remain on and online. This is a change in access to an existing agent, not evidence that the agent writes better code. [01-c1]

**Inline evidence — not spoken:** [Cursor announcement](https://cursor.com/changelog/remote-control-local-agents), item `feed:86e64baebef7f0e23a96adbb`, version `f0b87f5852d125e85cbeb2438fe5d0ee73e1a1bface9f1ea7031804286fb5ea1`; text locators: “You can now see and reply to the local agents running on your computer from the Cursor iOS app.” and “Your computer needs to stay on and online for remote control to work.”

**Visual direction:** Show `/security-review` as a text card. Separate it from a second card labeled “Organization push protection: private preview in the announcement.”

**Narration:**
Second, secret checking. GitHub announced a slash security-review command for Copilot CLI and Copilot App users, without requiring an organization’s GitHub Secret Protection plan. The announcement describes checking for secrets before a push. Do not confuse this developer-facing command with the organization push-protection feature that the same announcement described as being in private preview. These are distinct parts of the announcement, not interchangeable availability claims. [01-c2]

**Inline evidence — not spoken:** [GitHub secret-protection announcement](https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/secret-protection-must-scale-with-software/), item `feed:9d0ef8ba3ddce1b55a6dca3f`, version `8575119cd60816d0cd6c477201ca1ae2245015a6a27d45f5af8b9da87e6c352c`; text locators: “/security-review command for the Copilot CLI and Copilot App, so Copilot users can address secrets before a push even without needing an organization’s GitHub Secret Protection plan.” and “The feature is currently in private preview. Later this month, the feature will be available to organizations with GitHub Secret Protection across Enterprise Cloud and GitHub Teams. It will consume AI credits.”

**Visual direction:** Illustrative flame graph and source heatmap, labeled “Diagnostic views—not an optimization result.”

**Narration:**
Third, diagnosis. Simon Willison reports directing Codex to profile his web-edit Python app and produce a flame graph and heatmap. These are diagnostic views of where execution time is spent. The concrete result is an artifact to inspect, not a demonstrated optimization gain. His account shows an experienced developer choosing a diagnostic approach and asking an agent to carry it out. We do not know whether a beginner would obtain or interpret equally useful results. [01-c3]

**Inline evidence — not spoken:** [Willison’s profiling account](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/12/python-3-15-web-edit-profiling/), item `feed:26e4a943393a1b788d1e2dae`, version `de47f3a642088f8a087f0a6f46b95b49b6830aa108fd56ccd1dec0cf490cb5f8`; text locators: “I put the new Python 3.15 profiler through its paces by having GPT-6 Astra Extra High in Codex run it against my new web-edit app:” and “Here's the resulting example flame graph and heatmap.”

**Visual direction:** ReviewBench card: “219 pull requests · 187 public repositories · 19 languages.” Underneath: “Available evaluation resource ≠ proven fit for your project.”

**Narration:**
GitHub also launched ReviewBench, an available evaluation resource for code-review agents. Its reported corpus contains 219 pull requests from 187 public repositories across 19 languages. That provides something to evaluate against; its availability does not establish that a particular reviewer suits your small project. Large-repository workloads need not resemble a small script or single-file change. [01-c4]

**Inline evidence — not spoken:** [GitHub’s ReviewBench description](https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/reviewbench-an-open-benchmark-for-ai-code-review/), item `feed:9e3099b85951738510dd7533`, version `754cbbbbef0fdf63f52b8ef6428375ee7418da83b3001588ad78d50c265ee276`; text locators: “We built ReviewBench, a new code review offline benchmark, to address that gap, and it is available for you to use today.” and “ReviewBench contains 219 pull requests from 187 public open source licensed repositories spanning 19 languages, with its language and repository-size distributions closely matching GitHub overall.”

**Visual direction:** Return to the three columns. Add “Inspect the work” across all three, then a closing card: “Useful additions, not autonomous delivery.”

**Narration:**
The limitation runs across these examples. Cursor and GitHub establish their own announcements, not independent effectiveness. Willison describes his own app without a controlled comparison or complete accounting of effort. First-time users, accessibility users, and unsuccessful small-project attempts remain insufficiently represented. So assess these developments separately: supervision, secret checking, and diagnosis. Their practical value depends on whether you can inspect the resulting work and use the relevant check—not whether they share an agent label. [01-c5]

**Inline evidence — not spoken:** [Cursor](https://cursor.com/changelog/remote-control-local-agents), item `feed:86e64baebef7f0e23a96adbb`, version `f0b87f5852d125e85cbeb2438fe5d0ee73e1a1bface9f1ea7031804286fb5ea1`, text locator: “Your local agents appear in a list. Tap one to see what it's doing or send it a message.”; [GitHub](https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/secret-protection-must-scale-with-software/), item `feed:9d0ef8ba3ddce1b55a6dca3f`, version `8575119cd60816d0cd6c477201ca1ae2245015a6a27d45f5af8b9da87e6c352c`, text locator: “/security-review command for the Copilot CLI and Copilot App, so Copilot users can address secrets before a push even without needing an organization’s GitHub Secret Protection plan.”; [Willison](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/12/python-3-15-web-edit-profiling/), item `feed:26e4a943393a1b788d1e2dae`, version `de47f3a642088f8a087f0a6f46b95b49b6830aa108fd56ccd1dec0cf490cb5f8`, text locator: “Here's the resulting example flame graph and heatmap.”",

      "markdown": "# A successful signal is not necessarily successful software

As-of: 2026-10-14

**Presentation direction:** Planned for synthetic narration. Retain the spoken AI disclosure. Use labeled diagrams and attributed account cards. Evidence annotations are not spoken.

**Visual direction:** Split screen: “Reported success” on one side, “Delivered outcome” on the other. Display the date.

**Narration:**
This presentation uses AI-generated narration. As of October 14, 2026, the evidence supports a caution for individual developers: a successful signal is not necessarily successful software. A green job status, an addressed review comment, a familiar interface, and a low token price measure different things. None alone proves that the intended outcome was delivered and verified. The question is not whether agents can help, but what evidence supports a claim that their work is done.

**Visual direction:** Illustrative status card reading “Completed,” next to an empty review panel. Label “Acknowledged September 28 incident—not a current live demonstration.”

**Narration:**
Start with a specific delivery failure. In its October availability report, GitHub acknowledged a September 28 incident in which Copilot code review reported successful job completion without producing the review. That establishes a mismatch between status and output. It does not establish a general finding about review accuracy: a missing review and an incorrect review are different problems. But it shows why the completion label cannot substitute for checking that the requested output arrived. [02-c1]

**Inline evidence — not spoken:** [GitHub availability report](https://github.blog/news-insights/company-news/github-availability-report-september-2026/), item `feed:5942317efb2e306a353cac42`, version `2b8477c36458d01b02ef31fabffdfe1ae8339b51ac8a1407d7819528f05c4151`; text locator: “As a result, Copilot code review could not build a review, but reported that the job had completed successfully.”

**Visual direction:** Two metric cards: “Comment prompted a change” and “Change was correct.” Do not draw an equals sign between them.

**Narration:**
Evaluation has a separate gap. GitHub’s ReviewBench deliberately reduces tiny, single-file pull requests, which qualifies its relevance to many solo tasks. GitHub’s production addressed-rate metric measures whether a large language model judges that a review comment prompted a corresponding code change. It does not directly establish that the change was correct. A developer responding to a comment is an observable signal, but correctness is a different question. [02-c2]

**Inline evidence — not spoken:** [ReviewBench documentation](https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/reviewbench-an-open-benchmark-for-ai-code-review/), item `feed:9e3099b85951738510dd7533`, version `754cbbbbef0fdf63f52b8ef6428375ee7418da83b3001588ad78d50c265ee276`; text locators: “This reduces the overrepresentation of tiny, single-file changes while preserving more substantive, multi-file pull requests where review quality matters most.” and “Addressed rate, our online counterpart to precision, is the percentage of CCR comments that an LLM determines prompted a developer to make a corresponding code change, based on the diff, thread, reactions, resolution state, and post-review code.”

**Visual direction:** Attributed account card: “Fireship: FilmCraft editing attempt.” Show “Familiar interface” followed by “Reported playback lag / disappointing transitions.” Include “Video discloses Appify sponsorship.”

**Narration:**
Usability can diverge from appearance, too. Fireship reports attempting to edit a video in FilmCraft and encountering playback-related lag and disappointing transitions despite a familiar interface. This is an attributed usability failure, not a reproducible comparison, and it does not establish that AI caused the defects. Hardware and version details are missing. The video also discloses Appify sponsorship. Keep those limitations attached to the account, rather than turning it into a general verdict. [02-c3]

**Inline evidence — not spoken:** [Fireship video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wajoP_5Cpw8), item `youtube:wajoP_5Cpw8`, version `8744a09c189c7fe57c5beddc39f9817bb8e2d72e7bc3470320481ece2bd2220f`; segment locators: `s00060` (109.76–113.4 seconds), `s00063` (115.2–118.72 seconds), `s00068` (124.56–128.8 seconds), `s00074` (135.84–138.959 seconds), and `s00158` (298.919–303.4 seconds).

**Visual direction:** Separate cards for Lance and Vaishnavi’s team. Label “Different accounts—not a controlled comparison.”

**Narration:**
GitHub’s hackathon reporting offers another reminder about attribution. Participant Lance credits Copilot with creating a frontend and integrating an API in 30 minutes. Elsewhere, GitHub reports Vaishnavi’s team struggling with a movement-detection model. These are different accounts, not a controlled success-versus-failure comparison. Vaishnavi’s difficulty is not identified as a Copilot failure. Neither account tells us what a beginner working alone should expect. [02-c4]

**Inline evidence — not spoken:** [GitHub hackathon account](https://github.blog/developer-skills/career-growth/hack-the-world-why-hackathons-are-still-the-best-place-to-learn-to-build/), item `feed:4194b86040a10a4eac9e887c`, version `f6fa81764f870f94f07aec62e182fa40e3fc33d09536079532a0d241369c0820`; text locators: “GitHub Copilot was able to not only create a frontend in 30 minutes but also connects with the actual API itself and integrates it all together.
Lance, hackathon participant” and “Vaishnavi’s team spent part of the time fighting a model that couldn’t detect their movements. “Like, nothing is working,” Vaishnavi said at one point.”

**Visual direction:** Closing checklist: “Actual output,” “Representative behavior,” “Task-level expenditure.” Footer: “Independent comparisons and maintenance follow-up remain missing.”

**Narration:**
Finally, cost needs an outcome attached. Simon Willison argues that token prices are not readily comparable without knowing how many tokens a model consumes to achieve a goal in an agent workflow. That is not a measured small-project delivery study. Our qualified conclusion is to assess actual output, representative behavior, and task-level expenditure together. Independent controlled research, maintenance follow-up, and representative evidence for budget-constrained and accessibility users remain missing. Favorable signals are clues—not proof of verified delivery. [02-c5]

**Inline evidence — not spoken:** [GitHub availability report](https://github.blog/news-insights/company-news/github-availability-report-september-2026/), item `feed:5942317efb2e306a353cac42`, version `2b8477c36458d01b02ef31fabffdfe1ae8339b51ac8a1407d7819528f05c4151`, text locator: “As a result, Copilot code review could not build a review, but reported that the job had completed successfully.”; [Fireship](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wajoP_5Cpw8), item `youtube:wajoP_5Cpw8`, version `8744a09c189c7fe57c5beddc39f9817bb8e2d72e7bc3470320481ece2bd2220f`, segment locator `s00068` (124.56–128.8 seconds); [Willison’s cost discussion](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/13/llm-gemini/), item `feed:6ff0735dfa2a1786602e7b58`, version `a6cb93a068bca6b88086500d4f84badfd6255baa823a198066b04d6a8e160110`, text locator: “Prices like this aren't really comparable these days since what really matters is how many tokens a model takes to achieve a goal within an agentic harness.”",
      "claim_ids": [
        "02-c1",
        "02-c2",
        "02-c3",

        "02-c5"

      "piece_id": "03",
      "markdown": "# Make the next agent task bounded, inspectable, and affordable

As-of: 2026-10-14

**Presentation direction:** Planned for synthetic narration. Retain the spoken AI disclosure. Use readable file cards, checklists, and illustrative diagrams. Evidence annotations are not spoken.

**Visual direction:** Title card and date. Show a loop: “Define → Check → Inspect → Account for effort → Decide.”

**Narration:**
This presentation uses AI-generated narration. As of October 14, 2026, the strongest practical implication of the supplied evidence is modest: try one bounded agent task with explicit checks and a stopping budget before expanding autonomy. Record how to test it, inspect what arrives, and include correction and verification in the cost. This is a proposed evaluation workflow, not a proven productivity recipe. We do not have a comparison showing that it improves small-project completion rates.

**Visual direction:** File cards for `.github/copilot-instructions.md` and `.github/skills/quality-checks/SKILL.md`. Highlight “Test commands,” “What they check,” and “Troubleshooting.”

**Narration:**
Begin by making testing expectations explicit. For a Copilot repository, GitHub describes a repository instruction file where you can record expectations for testing and validation. It also describes a quality-checks skill that can explain which scripts run tests and linting, what they check, and how to troubleshoot failures. Linting means checking code against specified rules. These are places to record guidance—not proof that the agent followed it, or that any check ran and passed. [03-c1]

**Inline evidence — not spoken:** [GitHub repository guidance](https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/github-copilot-app-for-beginners-how-to-teach-copilot-about-your-codebase/), item `feed:f8fa0331a2b3ce4696b878a2`, version `a0ac872c91e89fad8413b83b3c5683bf89c547a0fcc88f0f3f56d7645592e8a3`; text locators: “Add a .github/copilot-instructions.md file to define guidance that applies across the repository, such as your preferred architecture, naming conventions, or expectations for testing and validation.” and “For example, a .github/skills/quality-checks folder could contain a SKILL.md file that explains:
- When Copilot should use the skill.
- Which scripts run the project’s tests and linting.
- What each script checks.
- How to troubleshoot common failures.”

**Visual direction:** Review checklist with separate boxes: “Status says complete” and “Review output exists.” Add an attributed September incident card.

**Narration:**
Next, inspect delivery. GitHub acknowledged a September incident in which Copilot code review reported successful completion without producing the review. It advised customers to request affected reviews again. So check whether your requested review actually arrived, instead of relying only on its status. For future reliability reporting, watch for evidence that reviews were delivered, not merely that jobs were labeled successful. Instructions and status indicators cannot replace looking at the output. [03-c2]

**Inline evidence — not spoken:** [GitHub availability report](https://github.blog/news-insights/company-news/github-availability-report-september-2026/), item `feed:5942317efb2e306a353cac42`, version `2b8477c36458d01b02ef31fabffdfe1ae8339b51ac8a1407d7819528f05c4151`; text locators: “As a result, Copilot code review could not build a review, but reported that the job had completed successfully.” and “We resolved the incident and advised customers to request affected reviews again.”

**Visual direction:** Diagram showing a main thread and worker thread feeding a profile. Label “Willison’s workload: 95.1% of stacks from AnyIO’s worker thread.”

**Narration:**
Diagnostic checks also need the right coverage. In Simon Willison’s web-edit profiling example, sampling all threads was essential: 95.1 percent of recorded stacks came from AnyIO’s worker thread and would have been missed by a main-thread-only profile. Threads are separate execution paths within an application. If you ask an agent to profile a threaded Python app, check that the profile includes the threads doing the work. Inspect its flame graph and heatmap before choosing an optimization. This is a conditional check, not a prediction of your bottleneck. [03-c3]

**Inline evidence — not spoken:** [Willison’s profiling account](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/12/python-3-15-web-edit-profiling/), item `feed:26e4a943393a1b788d1e2dae`, version `de47f3a642088f8a087f0a6f46b95b49b6830aa108fd56ccd1dec0cf490cb5f8`; text locators: “Sampling all threads was essential, since 95.1% of stacks came from AnyIO’s worker thread and would have been missed by a main-thread-only profile.” and “Here's the resulting example flame graph and heatmap.”

**Visual direction:** Attributed podcast cards: “Short tasks + check-ins” and “Longer orchestration exhausted usage.” Avoid universal quota or model-ranking graphics.

**Narration:**
Keep the first trial bounded. On HTML All The Things, one host describes short agent tasks with periodic check-ins. Another reports that longer orchestration burned through usage and prompted a return to smaller tasks. Those practitioner accounts support trying bounded work before assuming a subscription can sustain a longer cycle. They do not establish a universal quota, an ideal task duration, or a best model. [03-c4]

**Inline evidence — not spoken:** [HTML All The Things episode](https://www.htmlallthethings.com/podcast/ais-biggest-problem-isnt-intelligence-anymore), item `podcast:acc83661b4084b701efe6573`, version `d30ec05b567a9c16691e94f84c0c309050357ceea62781c3afa91b62697aed23`; segment locators: `s00081` (280.0400085449219–283.8399963378906 seconds), `s00088` (302.1199951171875–306.0400085449219 seconds), `s00136` (453.2799987792969–455.6400146484375 seconds), and `s00140` (461.79998779296875–465.7200012207031 seconds).

**Visual direction:** Trial record template: “Observable outcome / Checks / Retained outputs / Agent usage / Human testing and correction time / Stopping budget.” End on “Expand only after inspecting the whole cycle.”

**Narration:**
For your next trial, define one observable outcome, specify its checks, retain their outputs, and record agent usage alongside human testing and correction time. Expand only after examining that whole cycle. Instructions can be ignored, tests can miss bugs, and review adds effort that a solo developer must bear. Experienced practitioners’ judgment may not transfer to beginners. Start with checks you understand; another model’s agreement is not a substitute. The evidence to seek next is repeatable small-project results, including failures and total effort—not just prices or completion messages. [03-c5]

**Inline evidence — not spoken:** [GitHub repository guidance](https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/github-copilot-app-for-beginners-how-to-teach-copilot-about-your-codebase/), item `feed:f8fa0331a2b3ce4696b878a2`, version `a0ac872c91e89fad8413b83b3c5683bf89c547a0fcc88f0f3f56d7645592e8a3`, text locator: “Which scripts run the project’s tests and linting.”; [GitHub availability report](https://github.blog/news-insights/company-news/github-availability-report-september-2026/), item `feed:5942317efb2e306a353cac42`, version `2b8477c36458d01b02ef31fabffdfe1ae8339b51ac8a1407d7819528f05c4151`, text locator: “As a result, Copilot code review could not build a review, but reported that the job had completed successfully.”; [Willison’s cost discussion](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/13/llm-gemini/), item `feed:6ff0735dfa2a1786602e7b58`, version `a6cb93a068bca6b88086500d4f84badfd6255baa823a198066b04d6a8e160110`, text locator: “Prices like this aren't really comparable these days since what really matters is how many tokens a model takes to achieve a goal within an agentic harness.”; [HTML All The Things](https://www.htmlallthethings.com/podcast/ais-biggest-problem-isnt-intelligence-anymore), item `podcast:acc83661b4084b701efe6573`, version `d30ec05b567a9c16691e94f84c0c309050357ceea62781c3afa91b62697aed23`, segment locator `s00136` (453.2799987792969–455.6400146484375 seconds).",
      "claim_ids": [
        "03-c1",
        "03-c2",
        "03-c3",
        "03-c4",
        "03-c5"
      ]
    }
  ]
